claim: Conditional knockout of En1 and En2 in excitatory cerebellar nuclei neurons (eCN) leads to reduced postnatal growth of the cerebellar cortex in mice.
source: We found that conditional knockout of the mouse homeobox genes En1 and En2 in the excitatory cerebellar nuclei neurons (eCN) leads to reduced postnatal growth of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, and it is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: A subset of medial and intermediate eCN are lost in Atoh1-En1/2 CKO mutants.
source: A subset of medial and intermediate eCN are lost in the mutants, with an associated cell non-autonomous loss of their presynaptic partner Purkinje cells by birth leading to proportional scaling down of neuron production in the postnatal cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantification data in Figure 1Q showing specific reduction in medial and intermediate nuclei.

claim: Loss of eCN in Atoh1-En1/2 CKO mutants is associated with cell non-autonomous loss of their presynaptic partner Purkinje cells by birth.
source: A subset of medial and intermediate eCN are lost in the mutants, with an associated cell non-autonomous loss of their presynaptic partner Purkinje cells by birth leading to proportional scaling down of neuron production in the postnatal cerebellar cortex.
evidence: The abstract states this relationship, and Figure 7 shows temporal data supporting that PC loss follows eCN loss.

claim: Genetic killing of embryonic eCN throughout the cerebellum leads to loss of Purkinje cells and reduced postnatal growth throughout the cerebellar cortex.
source: Genetic killing of embryonic eCN throughout the cerebellum also leads to loss of Purkinje cells and reduced postnatal growth but throughout the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8 using the eCN-DTA model.

claim: The eCN play a key role in scaling the size of the cerebellum by influencing the survival of their Purkinje cell partners.
source: Thus, the eCN play a key role in scaling the size of the cerebellum by influencing the survival of their Purkinje cell partners, which in turn regulate production of granule cells and interneurons via the amount of sonic hedgehog secreted.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing the experimental findings from multiple mutant models.

claim: Purkinje cells regulate production of granule cells and interneurons via the amount of sonic hedgehog secreted.
source: Thus, the eCN play a key role in scaling the size of the cerebellum by influencing the survival of their Purkinje cell partners, which in turn regulate production of granule cells and interneurons via the amount of sonic hedgehog secreted.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Corrales et al., 2006; Corrales et al., 2004; De Luca et al., 2015; Fleming et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2004; Parmigiani et al., 2015; Wojcinski et al., 2017) in the Introduction and Results.

claim: Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs have a 31.2 ± 2.0% and 28.8 ± 4.1% reduction in cerebellar area in the vermis and paravermis, respectively, at P30.
source: We therefore determined whether the proportions of different neuron types was preserved in areas of the cerebellum with reduced size. As a proxy for analyzing cerebellum size, we quantified the area of mid-sagittal, paravermis and hemisphere sections of ~P30 animals, and found a 31.2 ± 2.0% and 28.8 ± 4.1% reduction in the vermis and paravermis, respectively but no reduction in the hemispheres of Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to littermate controls (En1lox/lox; En2lox/lox mice) (Figure 1A–G).
evidence: Quantitative data from measurements of cerebellar sections shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The anterior sector (ASec) and central sector (CSec) of the vermis are significantly decreased in area in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs by 37.1 ± 3.6% and 55.4 ± 2.7%, respectively.
source: When the vermis and paravermis were divided into three regions - an anterior sector (ASec), anterior to the primary fissure (lobules 1–5); a central sector (CSec), between the primary and secondary fissures (lobules 6–8); and a posterior sector (PSec), posterior to the secondary fissure (lobules 9–10), the PSec had no significant reduction, whereas the ASec and CSec were significantly decreased in area in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to littermate controls (ASec and CSec of the midline: 37.1 ± 3.6% and 55.4 ± 2.7%; paravermis: 25.0 ± 1.4% and 46.7 ± 7.0%) (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of sector areas shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The posterior sector (PSec) of the vermis has no significant reduction in area in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
source: When the vermis and paravermis were divided into three regions - an anterior sector (ASec), anterior to the primary fissure (lobules 1–5); a central sector (CSec), between the primary and secondary fissures (lobules 6–8); and a posterior sector (PSec), posterior to the secondary fissure (lobules 9–10), the PSec had no significant reduction, whereas the ASec and CSec were significantly decreased in area in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to littermate controls (ASec and CSec of the midline: 37.1 ± 3.6% and 55.4 ± 2.7%; paravermis: 25.0 ± 1.4% and 46.7 ± 7.0%) (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 1H showing no significant difference in PSec.

claim: The areas of the IGL and molecular layer are reduced only in the ASec and CSec of the vermis and paravermis in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs, and their proportions are well conserved compared to controls.
source: As predicted, in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs the areas of the IGL and molecular layer were reduced only in the ASec and CSec of the vermis and paravermis and their proportions were well conserved compared to controls (Figure 1I,J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E,G,H).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 1I,J and supplementary figures demonstrating proportional conservation.

claim: The numbers of Purkinje cells per midline section at P30 are reduced specifically in the ASec and CSec of the vermis by 31.0 ± 6.0% and 54.1 ± 7.5%, respectively, in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
source: The numbers of CALB1+ PCs per midline, paravermis or hemisphere section at ~P30 were indeed found to be reduced specifically in the ASec and CSec of the vermis (31.0 ± 6.0% and 54.1 ± 7.5% reduction, respectively) and paravermis (30.9 ± 7.9% and 37.7 ± 11% reduction, respectively), but their densities remained normal in all sectors of Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to controls (Figure 1K–M, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,I), indicating their numbers had scaled down proportionally.
evidence: Quantitative cell counts shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Purkinje cell densities remain normal in all sectors of the vermis in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to controls.
source: The numbers of CALB1+ PCs per midline, paravermis or hemisphere section at ~P30 were indeed found to be reduced specifically in the ASec and CSec of the vermis (31.0 ± 6.0% and 54.1 ± 7.5% reduction, respectively) and paravermis (30.9 ± 7.9% and 37.7 ± 11% reduction, respectively), but their densities remained normal in all sectors of Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to controls (Figure 1K–M, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,I), indicating their numbers had scaled down proportionally.
evidence: Density measurements shown in Figure 1M showing no significant differences.

claim: Granule cell densities are normal in all three sectors of the vermis in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
source: Similarly, quantification of NeuN-expressing granule cells showed that their densities were normal in all three sectors of the vermis (Figure 1N).
evidence: Density measurements shown in Figure 1N.

claim: The ratio of granule cells to Purkinje cells is preserved in the vermis of Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
source: Furthermore, the ratio of granule cells to PCs was preserved in the vermis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Ratio calculations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The ratio of interneurons to Purkinje cells or granule cells is preserved in the three sectors of Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to controls.
source: The ratio of interneurons to PCs or granule cells was preserved in the three sectors of Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K,L), although the density of Parvalbumin+ molecular layer interneurons was mildly increased in the ASec and CSec of mutants (1.2 ± 0.2 and 1.3 ± 0.1 fold, respectively, Figure 1O).
evidence: Ratio data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K,L.

claim: The density of Parvalbumin+ molecular layer interneurons is mildly increased in the ASec and CSec of Atoh1-En1/2 mutants by 1.2 ± 0.2 and 1.3 ± 0.1 fold, respectively.
source: The ratio of interneurons to PCs or granule cells was preserved in the three sectors of Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K,L), although the density of Parvalbumin+ molecular layer interneurons was mildly increased in the ASec and CSec of mutants (1.2 ± 0.2 and 1.3 ± 0.1 fold, respectively, Figure 1O).
evidence: Density measurements shown in Figure 1O.

claim: The major neuron types in the cerebellar cortex are scaled down regionally in numbers and the cell-to-cell ratios are well preserved in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
source: Thus, the major neuron types in the cerebellar cortex are scaled down regionally in numbers and the cell-to-cell ratios of the cortical neurons of the cerebellum are well preserved.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the quantitative data presented in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: The proportion of the EGL that contains the outer layer of proliferating GCPs at P7 is preserved in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs despite the EGL length being reduced in the ASec and CSec.
source: Indeed, quantification of the proportion of the EGL that contains the outer layer of proliferating GCPs at P7 showed that the ratio was preserved despite the EGL length being reduced in the ASec and CSec (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs have significant defects in motor behavior on the accelerating rotarod at both 1 month and 3 months of age.
source: The performance of mutants on trials of the accelerating rotarod over time showed a significant difference, as well as the cumulative measurement of performance in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs, with a shorter latency to fall compared to littermate controls at both ages (Figure 2A–B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Behavioral data shown in Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs do not have a significant decrease in grip strength compared to littermate controls at 3 months.
source: Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs did not have a significant decrease in grip strength compared to littermate controls at 3 months (Figure 2C) although they did at 1 month (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Grip strength measurements shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs have a significant decrease in stride length in footprint analysis of gait at both 1 month and 3 months of age.
source: In a footprint analysis of gait, mutant mice had a significant decrease in stride length at both ages (Figure 2D–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: Footprint analysis data shown in Figure 2D-E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs have motor behavior deficits despite the numbers of cells in the cerebellar cortical circuit being well scaled.
source: Thus, Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs have motor behavior deficits despite the numbers of cells in the cerebellar cortical circuit being well scaled.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating the behavioral data (Figure 2) with the cellular scaling data (Figure 1).

claim: There is an approximately 37.5 ± 4.6% reduction in the total number of large neurons in the cerebellar nuclei of Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to controls.
source: Stereology of Nissl-stained large neurons on every other coronal section of half cerebella of Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs and littermates revealed an ~37.5 ± 4.6% reduction in the total number of large neurons in the Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to controls.
evidence: Stereology quantification data shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: The loss of large neurons in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs is specific to the medial and intermediate nuclei.
source: Moreover, the loss of large neurons was specific to the medial and intermediate nuclei (Figure 1Q, Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Videos 1–2).
evidence: Stereology data shown in Figure 1Q and 3D reconstructions in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Videos 1-2.

claim: There is a correlation between the eCN that are reduced in number in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs and the areas of the cerebellum with a growth deficit in terms of PC projection maps.
source: Since PCs in the vermis and hemispheres project to the medial and intermediate CN (Leto et al., 2016), there is a correlation between the eCN that are reduced in number in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs and the areas of the cerebellum with a growth deficit (paravermis and vermis) in terms of the PC projection maps.
evidence: This is an inference based on known PC projection patterns cited from Leto et al., 2016 and the observed pattern of eCN loss.

claim: There is an estimated 1.4 ± 0.1 fold increase in the ratio of the number of PCs to eCN in the medial nucleus of Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to controls.
source: Interestingly, there was an estimated 1.4 ± 0.1 fold increase in the ratio of the number of PCs to eCN in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: Ratio calculation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1M.

claim: PC numbers did not fully scale down in proportion to the reduction in medial eCN in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
source: Thus, it appears that the PCs numbers did not fully scale down in proportion to the reduction in medial eCN.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased PC to eCN ratio shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1M.

claim: There is a preferential loss of the posterior part of the medial nucleus in Atoh1-En1/2 mutants.
source: Quantification of the medial CN that remained in Atoh1-En1/2 mutants compared to controls indicated that there is a preferential loss of the posterior part of the nucleus (see Videos 1 and 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: 3D reconstructions shown in Videos 1-2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Neurons of the more posterior region of the medial CN (fastigial oculomotor region) receive functional inputs from PCs in lobules 6 and 7 of the vermis.
source: Although a comprehensive study of topology based on the anterior-posterior position of PCs in lobules has not been published, it has been shown that neurons of the more posterior region of the medial CN (fastigial oculomotor region) receive functional inputs from PCs in lobules 6 and 7 of the vermis (Herzfeld et al., 2015; Noda et al., 1990; Sugihara et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Herzfeld et al., 2015; Noda et al., 1990; Sugihara et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2016).

claim: Labeled PCs in the ASec preferentially innervate the anterior medial CN.
source: Interestingly, we found that labeled PCs in the ASec preferentially innervated the anterior medial CN (Figure 3C–F), whereas labeled PCs from the CSec, the region with the greatest growth defect, innervated the posterior medial CN (Figure 3C,G–I).
evidence: Viral tracing data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Labeled PCs from the CSec innervate the posterior medial CN.
source: Interestingly, we found that labeled PCs in the ASec preferentially innervated the anterior medial CN (Figure 3C–F), whereas labeled PCs from the CSec, the region with the greatest growth defect, innervated the posterior medial CN (Figure 3C,G–I).
evidence: Viral tracing data shown in Figure 3C, G-I.

claim: Some labeled PCs in the vermis also target the intermediate CN.
source: Some labeled PCs in the vermis also targeted the intermediate CN (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Viral tracing data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: There could be a causal relationship between the extent to which the eCN are reduced in number in particular locations within each CN and the reduction in the number of their specific presynaptic PCs and associated lobule growth.
source: These results provide evidence that there could be a causal relationship between the extent to which the eCN are reduced in number in particular locations within each CN and the reduction in the number of their specific presynaptic PCs and associated lobule growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between PC projection patterns (Figure 3) and the pattern of eCN loss and cerebellar growth defects.

claim: En1/2 are expressed in subsets of all cerebellar cell types from as early as E8.5.
source: We previously showed that En1/2 are expressed in subsets of all cerebellar cell types from as early as E8.5 (Davis et al., 1991; Millen et al., 1995; Wilson et al., 2011) including in a small percentage of the medial TBR1+ eCN at E17.5 and granule cells primarily after they stop proliferating (Wilson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Davis et al., 1991; Millen et al., 1995; Wilson et al., 2011).

claim: Atoh1-Cre recombines in most eCN.
source: First, we confirmed that Atoh1-Cre recombines in most eCN by generating mice carrying Atoh1-Cre and the R26LSL-nTDTom reporter allele (Atoh1-nTDTom mice) and co-labeled for nuclear TDTom and three eCN markers (NeuN, MEIS2 protein and Slc17a6 RNA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-labeling experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: All but scattered TDTom+ cells in Atoh1-nTDTom mice express NeuN and the vast majority express Slc17a6 (vGlut2).
source: All but scattered TDTom+ cells expressed NeuN and the vast majority expressed Slc17a6 (vGlut2), and very few cells that expressed either marker did not express TDTom (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–R).
evidence: Co-labeling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-R.

claim: Almost all TDTom+ cells in Atoh1-nTDTom mice also express MEIS2, although at intermediate levels along the medial-lateral axis the co-labeling is less extensive.
source: Almost all TDTom+ cells also expressed MEIS2, although at intermediate levels along the medial-lateral axis the co-labeling was less extensive (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M–O).
evidence: Co-labeling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M-O.

claim: Almost all cells expressing Slc6a5 RNA (marker for glycinergic cells) or Gad1 (marker for inhibitory neurons) are negative for TDTom in Atoh1-nTDTom mice.
source: Furthermore, almost all cells expressing Slc6a5 RNA (marker for glycinergic cells) or Gad1 (marker for inhibitory neurons) were negative for TDTom (Figure 4—figure supplement 1S,T).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1S,T.

claim: All granule cells in the IGL of lobules anterior to lobule nine are labeled with TDTom in Atoh1-nTDTom mice, with only partial labeling in lobules 9 and 10, and no labeling of PCs or interneurons.
source: As expected, all granule cells in the IGL of the lobules anterior to lobule nine were labeled, with only partial labeling in lobules 9 and 10, and no labeling of PCs or interneurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: Labeling pattern shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1P.

claim: At E12.5, EN1/2 are expressed in the TDTom+ cells of the forming nuclear transitory zone in Atoh1-TDTom mice.
source: Using Atoh1-TDTom mice, we found that at E12.5, EN1/2 are expressed in the TDTom+ cells of the forming nuclear transitory zone that houses the newly born eCN and the PCs that have migrated away from the ventricular zone (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: At E15.5, high levels of EN1/2 are observed in TDTom+ cells in the medial and intermediate CN, whereas lateral CN show reduced expression in TDTom+ cells.
source: EN1/2 expression levels varied in eCN subpopulations as development progressed. At E15.5, high levels of EN1/2 were observed in TDTom+ cells in the medial and intermediate CN, whereas lateral CN showed reduced expression in TDTom+ cells (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: GCPs in the EGL and PCs express EN1/2 at high levels at E15.5.
source: GCPs in the EGL and PCs expressed EN1/2 at high levels at E15.5 (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: Only rare eCN express EN1 and not EN2 at E15.5.
source: Interestingly, only rare eCN expressed EN1 and not EN2 (Figure 4I–P).
evidence: Co-labeling with pan-EN and HA antibodies in En2HA/HA mice shown in Figure 4I-P.

claim: By E17.5, the majority of eCN cells have downregulated EN1/2, however scattered populations of TDTom+ cells continue to maintain strong expression, likely in the intermediate nuclei.
source: By E17.5, the majority of eCN cells had downregulated EN1/2, however scattered populations of TDTom+ cells continued to maintain strong expression, likely in the intermediate nuclei (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: At E17.5, EN1/2 are strongly expressed in the inner EGL, where postmitotic GCs reside.
source: At E17.5 EN1/2 were strongly expressed in the inner EGL, where postmitotic GCs reside (Figure 4H).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: In E13.5 Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs there is not yet a major decrease in EN1/2 protein in the eCN.
source: Finally, in E13.5 Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs there was not yet a major decrease in EN1/2 protein in the eCN (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Complete loss of EN1/2 protein in the eCN and EGL is observed by E15.5 in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs, whereas EN1/2 expression in the PCs does not appear altered.
source: However, complete loss of EN1/2 protein in the eCN and EGL was observed by E15.5, whereas as expected EN1/2 expression in the PCs did not appear altered (Figure 4Q–X).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4Q-X.

claim: EN1/2 are broadly expressed in both rhombic lip- and ventricular zone-derived cells of the cerebellum, however their expression is spatially and temporally dynamic.
source: Overall, this data shows that EN1/2 are broadly expressed in both rhombic lip- and ventricular zone-derived cells of the cerebellum, however their expression is spatially and temporally dynamic and EN1/2 expression is not lost in the eCN until E15.5 in mutants.
evidence: This is a summary of the expression data shown in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: EN1/2 expression is not lost in the eCN until E15.5 in Atoh1-En1/2 CKO mutants.
source: Overall, this data shows that EN1/2 are broadly expressed in both rhombic lip- and ventricular zone-derived cells of the cerebellum, however their expression is spatially and temporally dynamic and EN1/2 expression is not lost in the eCN until E15.5 in mutants.
evidence: This is based on the temporal analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4Q-X.

claim: Mutation of En1/2 specifically in GCPs (GCP-En1/2 CKO) does not lead to a reduction in cerebellar growth compared to littermate controls.
source: When the pharmacogenetic strategies were used to ablate En1/2 in Atoh1-tTA; tetO-Cre; En1lox/lox; En2lox/lox mice, we found that mutation of En1/2 specifically in GCPs (GCP-En1/2 CKO) did not lead to a reduction in cerebellar growth compared to littermate controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Deletion of En1/2 in embryonic eCN+GCPs (no Dox) or eCN alone results in a reduction in the area of the vermis and the paravermis but not the hemispheres compared to littermate controls.
source: Significantly, deletion of En1/2 in embryonic eCN+GCPs (no Dox) or eCN alone resulted in a reduction in the area of the vermis and the paravermis but not the hemispheres compared to littermate controls (Figure 5D–E), with the significant decrease being in the ASec (Figure 5F,M, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,G).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 5D-E, F, M and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,G.

claim: The areas of the IGL and molecular layer are reduced in the ASec of the vermis and paravermis and their proportions are conserved relative to the total area of each sector in both eCN+GCP-En1/2 and eCN-En1/2 CKOs.
source: The areas of the IGL and molecular layer were reduced in the ASec of the vermis and paravermis and their proportions were conserved relative to the total area of each sector in both eCN+GCP-En1/2 and eCN-En1/2 CKOs (Figure 5G,H,N,O and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E,J,K).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 5G,H,N,O and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E,J,K.

claim: The number of PCs are reduced in the ASec of the vermis and paravermis in both eCN+GCP-En1/2 and eCN-En1/2 CKOs, but PC densities are unchanged.
source: Similarly, the number of PCs were reduced in the ASec of the vermis and paravermis in both eCN+GCP-En1/2 and eCN-En1/2 CKOs, but PC densities were unchanged (Figure 5I,J,P,Q and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C,H,I).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 5I,J,P,Q and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C,H,I.

claim: No significant changes are observed in the densities of GCs and molecular layer interneurons (Pvalb+) in eCN+GCP-En1/2 and eCN-En1/2 CKOs.
source: We also did not observe any significant changes in the densities of GCs (Figure 5L,S) and molecular layer interneurons (Pvalb+) (Figure 5K,R).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 5K,L,R,S.

claim: The ratio of GCs or INs to PCs is conserved in both eCN+GCP-En1/2 and eCN-En1/2 mutants.
source: Finally, the ratio of GCs or INs to PCs was conserved in both mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F,L).
evidence: Ratio calculations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F,L.

claim: En1/2 are necessary in the eCN compartment of the rhombic lip-lineage to promote postnatal growth of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that En1/2 are necessary in the eCN compartment of the rhombic lip-lineage to promote postnatal growth of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparison of GCP-En1/2 CKO (no phenotype) versus eCN-En1/2 CKO (phenotype) shown in Figure 5.

claim: The numbers of interneurons and granule cells in the cerebellar cortex are scaled down proportionately to the number of PCs in eCN-En1/2 CKOs, likely through decreased SHH-stimulated proliferation of progenitors.
source: The numbers of interneurons and granule cells in the cerebellar cortex are scaled down proportionately to the number of PCs, likely through decreased SHH-stimulated proliferation of progenitors in eCN-En1/2 CKOs as in Atoh1-En1/2 CKO (Corrales et al., 2006; De Luca et al., 2015; Fleming et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2004; Wojcinski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the preserved cell ratios (Figure 5) and is supported by citations to previous work on SHH signaling (Corrales et al., 2006; De Luca et al., 2015; Fleming et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2004; Wojcinski et al., 2017).

claim: There is a 28.2 ± 2.8% and 30.0 ± 12.7% reduction in the total number of large neurons in the eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs and eCN-En1/2 CKOs, respectively, at P30.
source: Quantification of the number of large NeuN+ cells (cell area = 100–600 um2) on every other sagittal section of half of the ~P30 cerebellum (see Material and methods, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) showed a 28.2 ± 2.8% and 30.0 ± 12.7% reduction in the total number of large neurons in the eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs and eCN-En1/2 CKOs, respectively, and no change in the GCP-En1/2 CKOs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There is no change in the number of large neurons in GCP-En1/2 CKOs at P30.
source: Quantification of the number of large NeuN+ cells (cell area = 100–600 um2) on every other sagittal section of half of the ~P30 cerebellum (see Material and methods, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) showed a 28.2 ± 2.8% and 30.0 ± 12.7% reduction in the total number of large neurons in the eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs and eCN-En1/2 CKOs, respectively, and no change in the GCP-En1/2 CKOs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The mediolateral distribution in both eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs and eCN-En1/2 CKOs shows a significant preferential loss in medial and intermediate CN, similar to the Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
source: Furthermore, the mediolateral distribution in both eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs (Figure 6C) and eCN-En1/2 CKOs (Figure 6D) showed a significant preferential loss in medial and intermediate CN, similar to the Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs (Figure 6E and Figure 1Q).
evidence: Distribution data shown in Figure 6C,D,E.

claim: There is an estimated 1.5 ± 0.43 fold increase in the ratio of the number of vermal PCs in the ASec and CSec to the medial eCN in eCN-En1/2 CKOs.
source: Also, there was an estimated 1.5 ± 0.43 fold increase in the ratio of the number of vermal PCs in the ASec and CSec to the medial eCN in eCN-En1/2 CKOs (Figure 6G), although not significantly in the eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs compared to controls (Figure 6F).
evidence: Ratio calculation shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Deletion of En1/2 in GCPs leads to a mild differentiation defect.
source: We therefore used our mosaic mutant analysis approach to test whether production of GCs is altered when En1/2 are removed from scattered GCPs at P2. Indeed, we observed a significant decrease in the proportion of mutant cells (GFP+) in the inner EGL and IGL compared to controls, revealing that deletion of En1/2 leads to a mild differentiation defect in GCPs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3L–M).
evidence: Mosaic analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3L-M.

claim: A small reduction in cerebellar area (13.3 ± 5.3%) is observed at E17.5 in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to littermate controls but not at E15.5.
source: Quantification of the cerebellar area of mid-sagittal sections at E17.5 of mutants and controls revealed a small reduction in area in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs compared to littermate controls (13.3 ± 5.3%) but not at E15.5 (Figure 7A,F).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 7A,F.

claim: There appears to be a delay in the formation of the earliest fissures at E17.5 in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
source: In addition, there appeared to be a delay in the formation of the earliest fissures at E17.5 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Morphological observation shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: In control mice, 67.7 ± 3.8% of the TDTom+ cells express MEIS2 at E15.5 and 63.5 ± 3.5% at E17.5.
source: In control mice, 67.7 ± 3.8% of the TDTom+ cells expressed MEIS2 at E15.5 and 63.5 ± 3.5% at E17.5, and a similar percentage of TDTom+ cells expressed MEIS2 in mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: A similar percentage of TDTom+ cells express MEIS2 in Atoh1-TDTom-En1/2 CKO mutants compared to controls at E15.5 and E17.5.
source: In control mice, 67.7 ± 3.8% of the TDTom+ cells expressed MEIS2 at E15.5 and 63.5 ± 3.5% at E17.5, and a similar percentage of TDTom+ cells expressed MEIS2 in mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: None of the TDTom+ cells in Atoh1-TDTom mice express the PC marker FOXP2 at embryonic stages, confirming the selective labeling of rhombic lip lineage.
source: None of the TDTom+ cells expressed the PC marker FOXP2, confirming the selective labeling of rhombic lip lineage at embryonic stages (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Co-labeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: There is no significant change in the total number of MEIS2+ cells at E15.5 in Atoh1-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs compared to Atoh1-TDTom controls.
source: Quantification of the number of MEIS2+ cells on every other sagittal section of half of the cerebellum revealed no significant change in the total number of MEIS2+ cells at E15.5 in Atoh1-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs compared to Atoh1-TDTom controls (Figure 7O–P,S).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 7O-P,S.

claim: At E17.5, the MEIS2+ cells in the CN of Atoh1-TDTom-En1/2 CKO mutants are significantly reduced in number by 18.5 ± 1.6%.
source: At E17.5, the MEIS2+ cells in the CN of mutants were significantly reduced in number by 18.5 ± 1.6% (Figure 7Q–R,T).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 7Q-R,T.

claim: The distributions of MEIS2+ cells along the medial-lateral axis at E17.5 show a specific reduction in what will likely become the intermediate and medial nuclei in Atoh1-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs.
source: The distributions of the labeled cells along the medial-lateral axis showed a specific reduction in what will likely become the intermediate and medial nuclei (Figure 7T).
evidence: Distribution data shown in Figure 7T.

claim: TUNEL assay shows an increase in cell death in the region of the TDTom+ eCN population at E15.5 in Atoh1-TDTom-En1/2 mutants compared to controls and is still observable in some regions at E17.5.
source: TUNEL assay for cell death indeed showed an increase in cell death in the region of the TDTom+ eCN population at E15.5 in Atoh1-TDTom-En1/2 mutants compared to controls and was still observable in some regions at E17.5 (Figure 7G–N).
evidence: TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 7G-N.

claim: There is no decrease in the number of PCs per midline section at E15.5 in Atoh1-En1/2 CKO mutants compared to Atoh1-TDTom controls.
source: FOXP2 labeling of PCs revealed no decrease in the number of PCs per midline section at E15.5 in Atoh1-En1/2 CKO mutants compared to Atoh1-TDTom controls (Figure 7U).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 7U.

claim: At E17.5, there is a significant decrease (18.3 ± 1.1%) in the number of PCs per section in Atoh1-En1/2 CKO mutants.
source: At E17.5, however, there was a significant decrease (18.3 ± 1.1%) in the number of PCs per section (Figure 7V).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 7V.

claim: No increase in cell death is observed in either eCN-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs or in eCN+GCP-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs at E14.5 or E15.5 respectively.
source: Unlike Atoh1-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs, however, no increase in cell death was observed in either eCN-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs or in eCN+GCP-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs at E14.5 or E15.5 respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B,K,L).
evidence: TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B,K,L.

claim: At E17.5, TUNEL+ TdTom+ cells are detected in medial regions of both the eCN-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs and eCN+GCP-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs.
source: At E17.5, however TUNEL+ TdTom+ cells were detected in medial regions of both the eCN-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs and eCN+GCP-TDTom-En1/2 CKOs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,M).
evidence: TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,M.

claim: Quantification of MEIS2+ eCN at E17.5 shows a significant reduction in the medial eCN in the eCN-En1/2 CKOs compared to the littermate controls, but not in eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs.
source: Quantification of MEIS2+ eCN at E17.5, showed a significant reduction in the medial eCN in the eCN-En1/2 CKOs compared to the littermate controls, but not in eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D,N).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D,N.

claim: Mutants which have a reduced number of eCN at E17.5 compared to their littermate controls have increased TUNEL in the medial eCN.
source: However, we observed a large variation in the phenotype of different mutants (both eCN-En1/2 and eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs) and that mutants which had a reduced number of eCN at E17.5 compared to their littermate controls had increased TUNEL in the medial eCN (Figure 7—figure supplement 2F–H', P–S').
evidence: TUNEL and quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2F-H', P-S'.

claim: There is a delay in cell death in the eCN in the doxycycline-inducible En1/2 CKOs compared to Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs, likely resulting from a delay in induction of Cre expression.
source: This data shows that there is a delay in cell death in the eCN in the doxycycline-inducible En1/2 CKOs compared to Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs (Figure 7I,J), likely resulting from a delay in induction of Cre expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal comparison of cell death between Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs and the inducible CKOs shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: No reduction in cerebellar area or PC number per midline section is observed in the eCN-En1/2 or the eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs at E17.5.
source: Corresponding with the delay, we did not observe a reduction in cerebellar area or PC number per midline section in the eCN-En1/2 or the eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs at E17.5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2I,J,T,U).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2I,J,T,U.

claim: A normal number of eCN and PCs are produced in all the En1/2 CKOs that affect the eCN and a reduction in PC numbers is observed after eCN die.
source: In summary, a normal number of eCN and PCs are produced in all the En1/2 CKOs that affect the eCN and a reduction in PC numbers is observed after eCN die.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the temporal analysis of eCN and PC numbers shown in Figure 7 and supplements.

claim: When Atoh1-tTA; Atoh1-Cre; Igs7TRE-LtSL-DTA/+ mice are administered Dox starting at E13.5 (eCN-DTA mice) and analyzed at P30, a significant decrease in the number of eCN (41.2 ± 2.5%) is detected compared to littermate controls.
source: When Atoh1-tTA; Atoh1-Cre; Igs7TRE-LtSL-DTA/+ mice were administered Dox starting at E13.5 (eCN-DTA mice) and analyzed at P30, a significant decrease in the number of eCN was detected (41.2 ± 2.5%) compared to littermate controls (Igs7TRE-LtSL-DTA/+), and unlike in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs, the numbers were decreased across all three nuclei (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: In eCN-DTA mice, the eCN numbers are decreased across all three nuclei, unlike in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
source: When Atoh1-tTA; Atoh1-Cre; Igs7TRE-LtSL-DTA/+ mice were administered Dox starting at E13.5 (eCN-DTA mice) and analyzed at P30, a significant decrease in the number of eCN was detected (41.2 ± 2.5%) compared to littermate controls (Igs7TRE-LtSL-DTA/+), and unlike in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs, the numbers were decreased across all three nuclei (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 8B,C showing uniform distribution of loss across nuclei.

claim: The area of cerebellar sections and the number of PCs in eCN-DTA mice are reduced not only in the vermis and paravermis, but also in the hemispheres at P30.
source: Moreover, as predicted since the eCN are killed in all three CN, the area of cerebellar sections and the number of PCs in eCN-DTA were reduced not only in the vermis and paravermis, but also in the hemispheres at P30 (Figure 8D,I).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 8D,I.

claim: The proportions of IGL and ML area and the ratio of PCs to GCs are preserved in eCN-DTA mice, showing that a scaling down of the cerebellar cortex accompanies the loss of eCN.
source: Furthermore, the proportions of IGL and ML area and the ratio of PCs to GCs were preserved, showing that a scaling down of the cerebellar cortex accompanied the loss of eCN (Figure 8K–M).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 8K-M.

claim: The estimated ratio of vermal ASec and CSec PCs to medial eCN is increased 1.4 ± 0.3 fold in eCN-DTA mice.
source: The estimated ratio of vermal ASec and CSec PCs to medial eCN, however, was increased 1.4 ± 0.3 fold in eCN-DTA mice (Figure 8J).
evidence: Ratio calculation shown in Figure 8J.

claim: Analysis of TUNEL in eCN-DTA mice at E13.5 shows increased cell death in TDTom+ cells in the nuclear transitory zone and region of the CN.
source: Analysis of TUNEL in eCN-DTA mice at E13.5 (through E15.5) showed the expected increased cell death in TDTom+ cells in the nuclear transitory zone and region of the CN (Figure 8N–Q).
evidence: TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 8N-Q.

claim: PC numbers are normal at E15.5 in eCN-DTA mice, demonstrating that the reduction in PCs numbers seen at P30 is not a defect in neurogenesis.
source: Interestingly, PC numbers were normal at E15.5 (Figure 8R), demonstrating that the reduction in PCs numbers seen at P30 is not a defect in neurogenesis.
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 8R.

claim: When eCN are killed soon after they are generated, pre-synaptic partner PCs subsequently are reduced in number and then postnatal growth of the cerebellar cortex is proportionally decreased.
source: Thus, similar to En1/2 CKOs that include the eCN, when eCN are killed soon after they are generated, pre-synaptic partner PCs subsequently are reduced in number and then postnatal growth of the cerebellar cortex is proportionally decreased.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the eCN-DTA data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The survival of PCs is dependent on eCN, suggesting a retrograde regulation of cell viability.
source: Based on our finding that PCs scale down their numbers soon after eCN die in En1/2 CKOs and eCN-DTA mice, our study has provided evidence that the survival of PCs is dependent on eCN, suggesting a retrograde regulation of cell viability (Cowan et al., 1984).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal relationship between eCN loss and PC loss shown in Figures 7 and 8, and is supported by citation to the neurotrophic theory (Cowan et al., 1984).

claim: The timing of innervation of eCN by PCs fits with the proposal that PC survival is dependent on eCN, as axons from PCs extend into the CN by E15.5.
source: The timing of innervation of eCN by PCs fits with this proposal as axons from PCs extend into the CN by E15.5 (Sillitoe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work (Sillitoe et al., 2009) showing the timing of PC axon extension.

claim: In vitro assays have shown that PC survival is dependent on cell-cell interactions or on neurotrophins.
source: Furthermore, in vitro assays have shown that PC survival is dependent on cell-cell interactions (Baptista et al., 1994) or on neurotrophins (Lärkfors et al., 1996; Mount et al., 1995), and mouse mutants have shown that Bdnf and p75NTR null mutants exhibit cerebellar growth and foliation defects with some similarities to Atoh1-En1/2 mutants (Carter et al., 2003; Carter et al., 2002; Schwartz et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Baptista et al., 1994; Lärkfors et al., 1996; Mount et al., 1995; Carter et al., 2003; Carter et al., 2002; Schwartz et al., 1997).

claim: Bdnf is expressed specifically in the CN at E15.5, making it a good candidate for one of the eCN-derived survival factors for PCs.
source: Based on gene expression in the Allen Institute Database and our analysis in Atoh1-TDTom mice, Bdnf is expressed specifically in the CN at E15.5 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1); thus, it is a good candidate for one of the eCN-derived survival factor for PCs.
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and reference to Allen Institute Database.

claim: Gdnf is detected in the CN after birth, suggesting that it could also contribute to long-term survival of PCs in the cerebellum.
source: Gdnf is also detected in the CN after birth, suggesting that it could also contribute to long-term survival of PCs in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Gdnf expression patterns.

claim: Scaling of numbers between the eCN and PCs is not as precise as the scaling within the cerebellar cortex in all the mutants with a decreased number of embryonic eCN.
source: It appears that scaling of numbers between the eCN and PCs is not as precise as the scaling within the cerebellar cortex in all the mutants with a decreased number of embryonic eCN (En1/2 CKOs and eCN-DTA mutants).
evidence: This is inferred from the increased PC to eCN ratios shown in Figures 1, 6, and 8.

claim: The imprecise proportions of eCN and PCs could account for the motor behavior deficits observed in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
source: It is possible that the imprecise proportions of eCN and PCs accounts for the motor behavior deficits we observed in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs, although the smaller size of the cerebellum (~30% reduction) could also contribute as it might not be able to support all the long range neural circuits needed for full motor function.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed imprecise scaling and motor deficits.

claim: In a previous study, an approximately 20% reduction in the cerebellum without disruption of the cytoarchitecture did not lead to obvious motor defects.
source: In a previous study an ~20% reduction in the cerebellum without disruption of the cytoarchitecture did not lead to obvious motor defects, however the eCN and other cell types were not quantified and the reduction in size was less (Wojcinski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on citation to a previous study (Wojcinski et al., 2017).

claim: The higher than expected ratio of PCs in the vermis to the medial eCN might reflect the way in which scaling is established.
source: The higher than expected ratio of PCs in the vermis to the medial eCN might reflect the way in which scaling is established.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of scaling.

claim: GC and interneuron numbers depend on a precise and deterministic proliferative response to SHH downstream of PC number.
source: GC and interneuron numbers depend on a precise and deterministic proliferative response to SHH downstream of PC number (Corrales et al., 2006; De Luca et al., 2015; Fleming et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2004; Wojcinski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Corrales et al., 2006; De Luca et al., 2015; Fleming et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2004; Wojcinski et al., 2017).

claim: PC number depends on stochastic retrograde survival factors from the eCN.
source: In contrast, we propose that PC number depends on stochastic retrograde survival factors from the eCN.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the findings of the study.

claim: PC survival could be complicated by the convergence ratio of approximately 40 PCs to each eCN.
source: Moreover, PC survival could be complicated by the convergence ratio of ~40 PCs to each eCN (Person and Raman, 2011).
evidence: This is based on citation to a previous study (Person and Raman, 2011) showing the convergence ratio.

claim: eCN neurons maintain the survival of their presynaptic PC neurons.
source: As our model asserts that eCN neurons maintain the survival of their presynaptic PC neurons (Figure 9), we predict that eCN in the medial and intermediate nuclei that are lost in the greatest numbers in the Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs are preferentially innervated by PCs in the vermis and paravermis lobules, respectively, that exhibit the most diminution.
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: In eCN-DTA mice where eCN are killed evenly throughout the cerebellum, all regions of the cerebellum are similarly reduced in size.
source: Consistent with this, in eCN-DTA mice where eCN are killed evenly throughout the cerebellum, all regions of the cerebellum are similarly reduced in size.
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The foliation defects in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs are distinct from eCN- and eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs, which could be explained by the different Cre transgenes used targeting slightly different subsets of eCN or because of the delay in Cre expression using the tTA system.
source: Our finding that the foliation defects in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs are distinct from eCN- and eCN+GCP-En1/2 CKOs could then be explained by the different Cre transgenes used targeting slightly different subsets of eCN or because of the delay in Cre expression using the tTA system.
evidence: This is speculation about the differences between mutant phenotypes.

claim: PCs of the vermis central sector, where lobule growth and PC depletion are most pronounced in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs, preferentially innervate the posterior region of the medial CN that was also preferentially reduced in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
source: Determination of the projection pattern of PC axons into the CN showed that PCs of the vermis central sector, where lobule growth and PC depletion are most pronounced in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs, do indeed preferentially innervate the posterior region of the medial CN that was also preferentially reduced in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs.
evidence: This is based on the viral tracing data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The PCs of the ASec preferentially project to the anterior medial nucleus and part of the intermediate nucleus.
source: In a complementary fashion, the PCs of the ASec preferentially project to the anterior medial nucleus and part of the intermediate nucleus.
evidence: This is based on the viral tracing data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The first detected defect in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs is death of eCN starting at approximately E15.5, indicating that En1/2 are required in eCN for their survival in the embryo.
source: The first detected defect in Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs is death of eCN starting at ~E15.5, indicating that En1/2 are required in eCN for their survival in the embryo as EN1/2 protein is fully lost in the mutants by E15.5.
evidence: This is based on the temporal analysis of eCN loss and EN1/2 protein expression shown in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: This survival function of En1/2 is similar to the proposed function of the genes in other neurons in the brain.
source: This survival function of En1/2 is similar to the proposed function of the genes in other neurons in the brain (Fox and Deneris, 2012; Sonnier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Fox and Deneris, 2012; Sonnier et al., 2007).

claim: Conditional knockout of En1/2 in embryonic postmitotic serotonergic (5-HT) neuron precursors of the dorsal Raphe nucleus (DRN) results in a normal number of 5-HT neurons being initially generated, but the cells then become disorganized through abnormal migration and then a subset of cells undergo significant cell death around birth.
source: Conditional knockout of En1/2 in embryonic postmitotic serotonergic (5-HT) neuron precursors of the dorsal Raphe nucleus (DRN) results in a normal number of 5-HT neurons being initially generated, but the cells then become disorganized through abnormal migration and then a subset of cells undergo significant cell death around birth (Fox and Deneris, 2012).
evidence: This is based on citation to a previous study (Fox and Deneris, 2012).

claim: Mosaic analysis of the role of En1/2 in GCPs reveals only a mild function in promoting GCP differentiation, consistent with the expression of the EN proteins after birth mainly in the inner EGL where granule cells begin differentiating.
source: Mosaic analysis of the role of En1/2 in GCPs revealed only a mild function in promoting GCP differentiation, consistent with the expression of the EN proteins after birth mainly in the inner EGL where granule cells begin differentiating.
evidence: This is based on the mosaic analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3L-M and the expression data in Figure 4.

claim: Deletion of En1/2 in GCPs along with over-activation of SHH signaling results in a small increase in the proportion of mutant cells that remain in the proliferative GCP pool.
source: This role for En1/2 is consist with our recent finding that deletion of En1/2 in GCPs along with over-activation of SHH signaling results in a small increase in the proportion of mutant cells that remain in the proliferative GCP pool (Tan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citation to a recent study (Tan et al., 2018).

claim: Atoh1-Cre deletes En1/2 in the mossy fiber precerebellar nuclei, some of which express En1/2.
source: In addition to the RL-lineage, Atoh1-Cre deletes En1/2 in the mossy fiber precerebellar nuclei, some of which express En1/2.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Atoh1-Cre expression patterns.

claim: Most of the mossy fiber precerebellar nuclei, but not the inferior olive, are also targeted in eCN-En1/2 CKOs and eCN-DTA mice.
source: Most of the mossy fiber precerebellar nuclei, but not the inferior olive, are also targeted in eCN-En1/2 CKOs and eCN-DTA mice.
evidence: This is based on the Dox regimen and knowledge of when precerebellar nuclei are born.

claim: It is possible that some of the phenotypes (behavioral and cellular) seen in both Atoh1-En1/2 CKOs and eCN-DTA mice are a secondary (cell-nonautonomous) effect of loss of En1/2 or killing with DT of neurons outside the cerebellum.
source: Thus, it is possible that some of the phenotypes (behavioral and cellular) seen in both mutant types are a secondary (cell-nonautonomous) effect of loss of En1/2 or killing with DT of neurons outside the cerebellum.
evidence: This is speculation about potential confounding effects.

claim: If En1/2 are required in a subset of mossy fiber neurons for their survival, then their loss in En1/2 CKOs or eCN-DTA mice could result in death of their partner eCN.
source: If this is the case, one interpretation consistent with our hypothesis would be that eCN survival is dependent on neurotrophins secreted by precerebellar nuclei neurons. If En1/2 are required in a subset of mossy fiber neurons for their survival, then their loss in En1/2 CKOs or eCN-DTA mice could result in death of their partner eCN.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism.

claim: The scaling back of PCs would not likely be due to loss of mossy fiber neurons since PCs do not project to them.
source: The scaling back of PCs, however, would not likely be due to loss of mossy fiber neurons since PCs do not project to them.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of cerebellar circuit anatomy.

claim: En1 and En2 are required in the eCN after they are produced by the RL for the survival of a subset of medial/intermediate CN neurons, possibly the ones that normally express EN1/2 after E15.5.
source: In conclusion, En1 and En2 are required in the eCN after they are produced by the RL for the survival of a subset of medial/intermediate CN neurons, possibly the ones that normally express EN1/2 after E15.5.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the expression and loss-of-function data.

claim: Loss of a subset of medial/intermediate eCN neurons results in cell non-autonomous loss of the PCs that are their presynaptic partners in the vermis and paravermis.
source: Loss of a subset of medial/intermediate eCN neurons results in cell non-autonomous loss of the PCs that are their presynaptic partners in the vermis and paravermis (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: When eCN are killed in all three nuclei in eCN-DTA mutants, PC numbers are reduced in all regions of the cerebellum.
source: When eCN are killed in all three nuclei in eCN-DTA mutants, PC numbers are reduced in all regions of the cerebellum (Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The size of the cerebellar cortex is scaled back to be proportional to the number of PCs that remain in each region, producing a normal appearing cytoarchitecture.
source: The size of the cerebellar cortex is then scaled back to be proportional to the number of PCs that remain in each region, producing a normal appearing cytoarchitecture.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the scaling data shown in Figures 1, 5, and 8.

claim: The PCs do not appear to scale back fully to the number of the remaining eCN.
source: The PCs do not appear to scale back fully to the number of the remaining eCN.
evidence: This is based on the increased PC to eCN ratios shown in Figures 1, 6, and 8.

claim: Scaling of neurons in brain regions could be regulated by a combination of mitogens that stimulate proliferation of progenitors (neurogenesis) and survival factors that promote the survival of the neurons that are produced (neurotrophic theory) to help match synaptic partner neuron proportions.
source: Our results have important implications for how scaling of neurons in all brain regions could be regulated by a combination of mitogens that stimulate proliferation of progenitors (neurogenesis) and survival factors that promote the survival of the neurons that are produced (neurotrophic theory) to help match synaptic partner neuron proportions.
evidence: This is a broader implication inferred from the findings of the study.

claim: These proposed mechanisms of scaling could act in local or long distance brain circuits, as well as during evolution of mammals, possibly accounting for the parallel large expansion of the lateral eCN (dentate) and hemispheres in primates.
source: These proposed mechanisms of scaling could act in local or long distance brain circuits, as well as during evolution of mammals, possibly accounting for the parallel large expansion of the lateral eCN (dentate) and hemispheres in primates.
evidence: This is speculation about broader implications and evolutionary significance.
